name: Devonshire Quarrenden
history: An old West Country summer apple first recorded in 1678; it is usually credited to Devon, though the name may point to an origin near Carentan in Normandy. It is believed to be a parent of Worcester Pearmain.

look.description: Small, squat apple almost entirely covered in a dark crimson-purple flush, with a little green showing through.

taste.summary: Very juicy white flesh, sometimes stained pink under the skin, melting rather than crisp. The flavour is sweet, delicate and vinous rather than aromatic; a strawberry note shows in some fruit but is elusive and depends on picking at the right moment. Keeps only a few days.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-early Sep, straight from the tree

tree.notes: Fairly small, spreading, flat-topped tree that bears on spurs; crops well but can slip into alternate-year bearing.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (group 2) and partly self-fertile; blossom is vulnerable to frost, so pair with another early bloomer on a sheltered site.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp south-west England and similar cool maritime climates, where it has been grown for centuries.
climate.poor_climates: Frosty sites damage its early blossom; hot summers would make the soft early fruit go mealy even faster.

health.other: Reported to resist scab well, suiting wet western areas; early blossom is frost-tender. Fruit keeps only days.

grow_notes: A good early apple for wet western gardens. Avoid frost pockets because it blooms early, and pick and eat the fruit as it colours rather than storing it.

name: Dumelow's Seedling
history: Raised by a farmer named Dumelow or Dumeller at Shackerstone, Leicestershire; the original tree was growing by 1800. Shown as 'Dumelow's Crab' in 1818 and soon renamed 'Wellington', it was a leading Victorian keeping cooker and is a parent of Newton Wonder and Lane's Prince Albert.

look.description: Flattish, smooth, pale yellow apple with a light mottled red flush on the sunny side and a few russet dots.

taste.summary: Very firm, crisp, juicy white flesh that is intensely acid. Cooks down to a stiff, pale, strongly flavoured purée, ideal for mincemeat and sauces.

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing and a regular, good cropper.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate Britain, including the Midlands where it arose; reliably hardy.
climate.poor_climates: No record of use in hot climates; very short seasons may not ripen it for long keeping.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded in modern sources.

grow_notes: A dependable late cooker for a Midlands or northern garden. Pick in early October and store cool; the fruit keeps its acidity well into spring.

name: Early Victoria
history: Raised by William Lynn at Emneth in the Wisbech fruit district and introduced by Cross of Wisbech; it gained an RHS Award of Merit in 1899. Officially catalogued as Emneth Early, it remains one of the standard early codlin-type cookers.

look.description: Tall, ribbed, conical codlin apple in plain pale green ripening to yellow-green.

taste.summary: Very tart greenish flesh that is crisp only straight from the tree and soon softens. Cooks quickly to a light, frothy purée and dries well into rings; left to ripen to pale yellow it becomes a passable eating apple with a faint, sweet floral scent. Does not keep.
taste.best_eaten: Cook from late Jul to Aug; thinnings usable from July

tree.notes: Sets very heavily; thin the fruit hard (use the thinnings for cooking) or it falls into biennial bearing.

pollination.notes: Group 3; partly self-fertile but sets better with a group 2-4 partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate Britain, including the north; an early cooker that ripens even in short seasons.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would make the soft early fruit go mealy quickly; little use where cooking apples are needed late.

health.other: Main problem is strong biennial bearing if not thinned; disease scores not well recorded.

grow_notes: Good early cooker for small gardens. Thin heavily in early summer to keep it cropping every year, and pick over several weeks from late July.

name: Edward VII
history: First recorded in 1902 and introduced by the Rowe nursery of Worcester in 1908; it won an RHS Award of Merit in 1903. Its very late blossom has made it a favourite for frosty sites, and it holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Fairly large, smooth, broad-conical apple, pale green ripening yellow, occasionally with a faint flush.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse, fairly juicy white flesh with a brisk acidity; an excellent late cooker that makes a well-flavoured purée.

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing and a regular cropper; one of the best choices for frost pockets because of its very late flowering.

pollination.notes: Very late flowering (group 6); needs another late bloomer such as Court Pendu Plat or a group 5 variety.

climate.best_climates: Cool, frost-prone temperate areas of Britain and northern Europe, where late blossom escapes spring frosts.
climate.poor_climates: Short cold seasons may not ripen it for storage; hot climates unrecorded.

health.other: Very resistant to scab and generally healthy; suitable for organic growing.

grow_notes: The obvious cooker for cold, frosty gardens. Pair it with another late-flowering variety, pick in mid-October and store for use through winter into spring.

name: Fortune
history: Bred in 1904 by Laxton Brothers of Bedford and released in 1931 as Laxton's Fortune; it received an RHS First Class Certificate in 1948. Not to be confused with the American 'Fortune' released by Cornell (Geneva) in 1995.

look.description: Neat, slightly conical apple, greenish-yellow streaked and flushed with bright red.

taste.summary: Fairly firm, slightly coarse, juicy cream flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavour that hints at its Cox parent; best eaten fresh in early autumn.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous spur-bearer; tends to crop in alternate years unless thinned in heavy years.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate Britain and similar maritime climates.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers likely to soften the fruit and reduce colour; untested in warm regions.

health.other: Prone to canker on heavy, wet soils; biennial cropping is the other main drawback.

grow_notes: A good early-autumn eater for well-drained soil. Thin heavy crops to break the biennial habit and keep an eye out for canker.
